title: Present Simple

revision.summary: Master the present simple for routines, facts, questions, negatives, frequency and third-person -s.

body_content:
Present Simple — the everyday tense

Use the present simple for routines, habits, repeated actions, facts, schedules, and things that are generally true. Think: What happens regularly?

1. Positive sentences

With I, you, we, they, use the base verb:

  • I work in Accra.
  • You study English every day.
  • We play football on Saturdays.
  • They live near the school.

With he, she, it, usually add -s:

  • He works in a bank.
  • She studies English every evening.
  • It rains a lot here.

2. The third-person -s rules

  • Most verbs: work → works, read → reads, play → plays.
  • Verbs ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -o: add -es: watch → watches, go → goes, fix → fixes.
  • Consonant + y: change y → ies: study → studies, try → tries.
  • Vowel + y: keep y: play → plays, enjoy → enjoys.

3. Negative sentences

Use do not / don't with I/you/we/they and does not / doesn't with he/she/it. After doesn't, the main verb returns to its base form.

  • I don't work on Sunday.
  • They don't watch TV every night.
  • He doesn't work on Sunday. Not: doesn't works.
  • She doesn't like coffee.

4. Questions

Put Do or Does before the subject:

  • Do you speak English?
  • Do they live here?
  • Does he play football?
  • Does she study every day?

Short answers: Yes, I do. / No, I don't. / Yes, he does. / No, she doesn't.

5. Frequency words

Common words are always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never. They normally come before the main verb: I usually walk to work. She often reads at night. With be, the frequency word normally comes after be: He is always early.

6. Time expressions

Present simple often appears with every day, every week, on Mondays, in the morning, at weekends, once a month.

  • I exercise every morning.
  • We visit our family on Sundays.
  • She has an English class twice a week.

7. Facts and general truths

  • Water boils at 100°C.
  • The sun rises in the east.
  • Birds have wings.

Common mistakes

Watch the helper verb.
He works here. → Does he work here?
He doesn't work here.

Don't use -s after does/doesn't. The does already carries the third-person grammar.

Quick pattern

Positive: Subject + verb (+s for he/she/it).
Negative: Subject + don't/doesn't + base verb.
Question: Do/Does + subject + base verb?

title: Be: am/is/are

revision.summary: Master am, is and are for identity, jobs, location, age, feelings, descriptions, negatives and questions.

body_content:
Be: am / is / are — the verb that connects

The verb be is one of the most important English verbs. In the present tense it changes to am, is, or are. Use it to talk about identity, description, age, location, feelings, jobs, and states.

1. Choose the correct form

  • I am ready.
  • You are my friend.
  • He is a teacher.
  • She is happy.
  • It is cold.
  • We are at home.
  • They are students.

2. The core pattern

I → am
He / She / It → is
You / We / They → are

3. Contractions

  • I am → I'm
  • He is → He's
  • She is → She's
  • It is → It's
  • You are → You're
  • We are → We're
  • They are → They're

4. Uses of be

  • Identity: I am Daniel. She is my sister.
  • Job: He is a doctor. They are teachers.
  • Location: We are at school. The keys are on the table.
  • Feelings/states: I am tired. You are hungry.
  • Age: I am 20 years old. She is ten.
  • Description: The room is small. They are friendly.

5. Negative sentences

Add not after am/is/are:

  • I am not tired.
  • He is not at work.
  • She isn't angry.
  • We aren't late.
  • They aren't from Ghana.

Notice that we do not use do/does with be: She isn't happy. Not: She doesn't be happy.

6. Questions with be

Move am/is/are before the subject:

  • Am I late?
  • Is he your brother?
  • Is she at home?
  • Are you ready?
  • Are they students?

Short answers: Yes, I am. / No, I'm not. / Yes, he is. / No, he isn't. / Yes, they are. / No, they aren't.

7. Be vs. ordinary verbs

Use be for a state or identity: She is tired. Use an ordinary verb for an action: She works every day.

  • He is a teacher. → identity/job
  • He teaches English. → action
  • They are at home. → location
  • They watch TV. → action

Common mistakes

Match the subject and be.
I am happy. ✓
She is happy. ✓
They are happy. ✓

Don't add do/does. Are you ready? ✓   Do you are ready? ✗

Quick pattern

Positive: Subject + am/is/are + complement.
Negative: Subject + am/is/are + not + complement.
Question: Am/Is/Are + subject + complement?

title: Pronouns

revision.summary: Use subject pronouns (I, you, he, she, it, we, they) and object pronouns (me, you, him, her, it, us, them) correctly in simple sentences.
examples: I like her. She likes me.

body_content:
Pronouns — subject and object

A pronoun replaces a noun so we don't repeat it. Subject pronouns (I, you, he, she, it, we, they) come before the verb and show who does the action. Object pronouns (me, you, him, her, it, us, them) come after the verb or a preposition and show who receives the action.

1. Subject pronouns

  • I like coffee.
  • She works here.
  • They live near the school.

2. Object pronouns

  • I like her.
  • He calls him every day.
  • Give it to me, please.

Note that you and it don't change form between subject and object.

Quick check

  1. ___ love coffee. (I / me) → I
  2. Can you help ___? (I / me) → me
  3. She sees ___ every day. (they / them) → them

title: Prepositions of Time

revision.summary: Use in, on and at correctly with time expressions such as clock times, days and longer periods.
examples: Let's meet at noon, on Friday.

body_content:
Prepositions of Time — in, on, at

Use at with clock times and a few fixed expressions (at 7 o'clock, at night, at the weekend). Use on with days and dates (on Monday, on 5 May). Use in with longer periods (in the morning, in July, in 2024, in winter).

Examples

  • I wake up at 7 o'clock.
  • We have class on Monday.
  • She was born in 1990.
  • My birthday is in June.
  • Let's meet at noon, on Friday.

Quick check

  1. I have lunch ___ 1 o'clock. → at
  2. Her party is ___ Saturday. → on
  3. It's very cold ___ winter. → in

title: Linking Words: and, but, because, or

revision.summary: Join two simple ideas using and, but, because and or.
examples: I stayed home because it was raining.
Do you want tea or coffee?
He works hard, but he doesn't earn much.

body_content:
Linking Words — and, but, because, or

And adds information. But shows contrast. Because gives a reason. Or gives a choice or alternative.

Examples

  • I like tea and coffee.
  • She is tired but happy.
  • I stayed home because it was raining.
  • Do you want tea or coffee?
  • He works hard, but he doesn't earn much.

Quick check

  1. Combine: "It was cold. I wore a coat." (because) → I wore a coat because it was cold.
  2. Combine: "She is young. She is very wise." (but) → She is young but very wise.
  3. Choose: Do you want juice ___ water? → or

title: Too and Very

revision.summary: Use too and very to describe degree, and know when too signals a problem.
examples: This coffee is very hot. / This coffee is too hot to drink.
The shoes are too small for me.
It's very cold today. / It's too cold to swim.

body_content:
Too and Very

Very simply makes an adjective stronger (very tired = really tired). Too means more than necessary, and it usually causes a problem (too tired = so tired that you can't do something).

Examples

  • This coffee is very hot. / This coffee is too hot to drink.
  • She is very kind.
  • The shoes are too small for me.
  • It's very cold today. / It's too cold to swim.

Quick check

  1. The bag is ___ heavy — I can't lift it. → too
  2. She is ___ happy today. → very
  3. This box is ___ big to fit in the car. → too

title: Short-Form Answers

revision.summary: Answer yes/no questions naturally using the subject plus the matching auxiliary verb (am/is/are, do/does, can).
examples: Are you a teacher? Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
Does she speak English? Yes, she does. / No, she doesn't.
Can you swim? Yes, I can. / No, I can't.
Is it raining? Yes, it is.
Do they live here? No, they don't.

body_content:
Short-Form Answers

Instead of repeating the whole question, English speakers usually answer with a short form: the subject + the same auxiliary verb (am/is/are, do/does, can) + not (for "no").

Examples

  • Are you a teacher? Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
  • Does she speak English? Yes, she does. / No, she doesn't.
  • Can you swim? Yes, I can. / No, I can't.
  • Is it raining? Yes, it is.
  • Do they live here? No, they don't.

Quick check

  1. Are you tired? → Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
  2. Does he play football? → Yes, he does. / No, he doesn't.
  3. Can they cook? → Yes, they can. / No, they can't.

title: Going To — Future Plans

revision.summary: Use be + going to + base verb to talk about plans and intentions already decided.
examples: I am going to visit my parents this weekend.
She is going to study medicine.
We are not going to travel this year.
Are you going to call him?
What are you going to do tonight?

body_content:
Going To — Future Plans

Use be + going to + base verb for something you have already decided to do in the future.

Examples

  • I am going to visit my parents this weekend.
  • She is going to study medicine.
  • We are not going to travel this year.
  • Are you going to call him?
  • What are you going to do tonight?

Quick check

  1. I ___ (going to / study) tonight. → am going to study
  2. She ___ (not / going to / come). → is not going to come
  3. ___ you going to visit them? → Are

title: Will — Offers

revision.summary: Use I'll + base verb to offer to do something for someone, decided at the moment of speaking.
examples: I'll carry that bag for you.
I'll help you with your homework.
Don't worry, I'll call the doctor.

body_content:
Will — Offers

Use I'll + base verb to offer to do something for someone, decided at the moment of speaking — not a plan made earlier (that's going to).

Examples

  • I'll carry that bag for you.
  • I'll help you with your homework.
  • Don't worry, I'll call the doctor.
  • I'll open the window.
  • I'll get you some water.

Quick check

  1. Your friend looks cold. Offer to close the window: → I'll close the window.
  2. Someone drops their books. Offer to help: → I'll help you.
  3. Choose the offer, not the plan: "I'll call you later" / "I'm going to call you next week" → I'll call you later.

title: Adverbs of Frequency

revision.summary: Say how often something happens using always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely and never, in the correct word order.
examples: We sometimes go to the cinema.

body_content:
Adverbs of Frequency

Adverbs of frequency usually go before the main verb, but after the verb "be." Rough order from most to least often: always → usually → often → sometimes → rarely → never.

Examples

  • I always brush my teeth.
  • She is usually happy.
  • We sometimes go to the cinema.
  • He never eats meat.
  • They often visit their grandparents.

Quick check

  1. Put in order: "coffee / drinks / never / he" → He never drinks coffee.
  2. Put in order: "tired / is / usually / she" → She is usually tired.
  3. Choose the correct position: "I sometimes am late" or "I am sometimes late"? → I am sometimes late.

title: Imperatives

revision.summary: Give simple instructions, commands and warnings using the base verb, and don't for negatives.

body_content:
Imperatives

Use the base verb to give an instruction. Add don't to make it negative. Common for directions, instructions, warnings and advice.

Examples

  • Open your book.
  • Close the door, please.
  • Don't touch that!
  • Turn left at the corner.
  • Be careful!

Quick check

  1. Give an instruction to open a window → Open the window.
  2. Give a warning about hot food → Be careful, it's hot!
  3. Give a negative instruction about talking in class → Don't talk in class.

title: Present Continuous

revision.summary: Describe what is happening right now using am/is/are + verb-ing, and tell it apart from the present simple.
examples: I am writing an email right now.

body_content:
Present Continuous

Use am/is/are + verb-ing for actions happening now or around now. The present simple, by contrast, describes routines and general facts.

Examples

  • I am writing an email right now.
  • She is cooking dinner.
  • They are watching a movie.
  • He is not sleeping.
  • What are you doing?

Quick check

  1. Right now: She ___ (read) a book. → is reading
  2. Choose simple or continuous: "I usually ___ (walk) to work" → walk
  3. Choose simple or continuous: "Look! It ___ (rain)" → is raining

title: Comparatives

revision.summary: Compare two things using -er / more...than, depending on the length of the adjective.
examples: My car is faster than yours.
This book is more interesting than that one.
She is taller than her brother.
This exercise is easier than the last one.

body_content:
Comparatives

Short adjectives add -er (+ than). Adjectives ending in -y change to -ier. Longer adjectives use more ... than.

Examples

  • My car is faster than yours.
  • This book is more interesting than that one.
  • She is taller than her brother.
  • This exercise is easier than the last one.
  • Winter is colder than summer.

Quick check

  1. big → ___ than → bigger than
  2. expensive → ___ than → more expensive than
  3. happy → ___ than → happier than

title: Superlatives and Irregular Adverbs

revision.summary: Describe the extreme of a group using superlatives, and use a few irregular adverbs (good→well, fast, hard) correctly.
examples: She is the tallest student in the class.
This is the most interesting book I've read.

body_content:
Superlatives and Irregular Adverbs

Short adjectives add -est (the ...est). Longer adjectives use the most .... A few common adverbs don't end in -ly and are irregular: good → well, fast → fast, hard → hard.

Examples

  • She is the tallest student in the class.
  • This is the most interesting book I've read.
  • He runs fast. (not "fastly")
  • She works hard.
  • He speaks English well. (not "goodly")

Quick check

  1. tall → the ___ → the tallest
  2. beautiful → the ___ → the most beautiful
  3. Choose: "She sings very ___" (good/well) → well

title: Numbers and Money

revision.summary: Use cardinal and ordinal numbers, and talk about prices and money.
examples: She lives on the fifth floor.
How much is a coffee here?
It's my first day at work.

body_content:
Numbers and Money

Cardinal numbers (one, two, three...) count things. Ordinal numbers (first, second, third...) show order or position. For money, say the amount then the currency (five dollars, ten euros), and use "How much is/are...?" to ask a price.

Examples

  • I have three brothers.
  • She lives on the fifth floor.
  • This costs twenty dollars.
  • How much is a coffee here?
  • It's my first day at work.

Quick check

  1. Turn into an ordinal: four → ___ → fourth
  2. How do you ask a price? ___ is this bag? → How much
  3. Say the price: $15 → ___ → fifteen dollars

title: Countries, Nationalities and Languages

revision.summary: Talk about where people are from, their nationality, and what language they speak.
examples: He is Japanese. He speaks Japanese.
She speaks two languages: English and Portuguese.

body_content:
Countries, Nationalities and Languages

A country name is a place (France, Japan). A nationality describes a person from that country (French, Japanese). The language people speak often has the same word as the nationality (She speaks French).

Examples

  • I'm from Brazil. I'm Brazilian.
  • He is Japanese. He speaks Japanese.
  • They come from Spain.
  • What nationality are you?
  • She speaks two languages: English and Portuguese.

Quick check

  1. Brazil → ___ → Brazilian
  2. Japan → nationality: ___ → Japanese
  3. Complete: I ___ from Italy. I'm Italian. → come

title: Telling the Time and Days

revision.summary: Say the time and the days of the week.

body_content:
Telling the Time and Days

To tell the time, say the hour first, then the minutes (it's three fifteen, it's half past three). The days of the week are Monday to Sunday. Use "on" with days (on Monday).

Examples

  • It's nine o'clock.
  • It's half past six.
  • It's a quarter to five.
  • My class is on Tuesday.
  • What day is it today?

Quick check

  1. 3:30 → It's ___ → half past three
  2. Order: Monday, ___, Wednesday → Tuesday
  3. Ask the time politely: Excuse me, ___? → what time is it

title: Dates, Months and Years

revision.summary: Say dates, the months of the year, and years.
examples: Today is the tenth of March.

body_content:
Dates, Months and Years

Months go from January to December. To say a date, use the ordinal number for the day (the fifth of May / May fifth) and "in" for the month or year alone.

Examples

  • My birthday is in July.
  • Today is the tenth of March.
  • She was born in 2001.
  • Christmas is in December.
  • What's the date today?

Quick check

  1. Which month comes after June? → ___ → July
  2. Say the date: 5 May → the ___ of May → fifth
  3. I was born ___ 1998. (in/on) → in

title: Seasons and Weather

revision.summary: Name the four seasons and describe the weather.

body_content:
Seasons and Weather

The seasons are spring, summer, autumn (fall) and winter. Common weather words are sunny, rainy, cloudy, windy, snowy, hot and cold. Use "It's..." to describe weather.

Examples

  • It's sunny today.
  • It's cold in winter.
  • It often rains in autumn.
  • Summer is hot here.
  • It's snowing outside.

Quick check

  1. Which season is coldest? → ___ → winter
  2. Describe rain weather: It's ___. → rainy
  3. Order the seasons starting with spring → spring, summer, autumn, winter

title: Shops and Places in Town

revision.summary: Name common shops and places in town, and say where to go for something.
examples: I need to go to the bakery.
Where can I buy stamps? At the post office.

body_content:
Shops and Places in Town

Common places include the supermarket, bakery, pharmacy, bank, post office and park. Use "Where can I buy...?" or "Where is the...?" to ask about a place.

Examples

  • I need to go to the bakery.
  • Where is the nearest pharmacy?
  • She works at the bank.
  • Let's meet at the park.
  • Where can I buy stamps? At the post office.

Quick check

  1. Where do you buy bread? → the ___ → bakery
  2. Where do you buy medicine? → the ___ → pharmacy
  3. Ask about a place: ___ is the supermarket? → Where

title: Interests and Sports

revision.summary: Talk about hobbies, interests and sports you play or like.
examples: He does yoga twice a week.

body_content:
Interests and Sports

Use "play" with team sports and ball games (play football, play tennis), "go" with -ing activities (go swimming, go running), and "do" with other activities (do yoga). Use "like/love/enjoy" + -ing to talk about interests.

Examples

  • I play basketball on weekends.
  • She goes swimming every morning.
  • He does yoga twice a week.
  • I love reading books.
  • They enjoy playing video games.

Quick check

  1. play, go or do: ___ football → play
  2. play, go or do: ___ swimming → go
  3. play, go or do: ___ yoga → do

title: Everyday Activities

revision.summary: Describe daily activities and how often you do them, using the present simple.
examples: I get up at seven every day.
She usually has breakfast at home.
We sometimes go to the gym after work.
They go to bed early on weekdays.

body_content:
Everyday Activities

Everyday activities include things like getting up, having breakfast, going to work/school, and going to bed. Combine them with frequency words (always, usually, sometimes, never) to say how often.

Examples

  • I get up at seven every day.
  • She usually has breakfast at home.
  • We sometimes go to the gym after work.
  • He never skips breakfast.
  • They go to bed early on weekdays.

Quick check

  1. I ___ (get up) at 7 every day. → get up
  2. She ___ (have) lunch at school. → has
  3. Add a frequency word: I ___ go to the gym. → sometimes

title: Jobs

They work for a big company.

body_content:
Jobs

Use "He/She is a..." + job title, and "He/She works as a..." / "He/She works at/for..." + place. Ask "What do you do?" to ask about someone's job.

Examples

  • She is a teacher.
  • He works as a chef.
  • I work at a hospital.
  • What do you do? I'm an engineer.
  • They work for a big company.

Quick check

  1. She is a ___ (teaches at school). → teacher
  2. Ask about someone's job: What ___ you do? → do
  3. He works ___ a nurse. (as/at) → as

title: The Home: Rooms and Furniture

revision.summary: Name rooms in a house and the furniture found in them, using there is/there are.
examples: There is a bed in the bedroom.
There are two chairs in the kitchen.
The sofa is in the living room.
Is there a wardrobe in your room?
There isn't a bath in the bathroom, only a shower.

body_content:
The Home: Rooms and Furniture

Common rooms: kitchen, bedroom, bathroom, living room. Common furniture: bed, table, chair, sofa, wardrobe. Use "there is" (singular) and "there are" (plural) to say what's in a room.

Examples

  • There is a bed in the bedroom.
  • There are two chairs in the kitchen.
  • The sofa is in the living room.
  • Is there a wardrobe in your room?
  • There isn't a bath in the bathroom, only a shower.

Quick check

  1. There ___ a table in the kitchen. (is/are) → is
  2. There ___ four chairs. (is/are) → are
  3. Where do you sleep? In the ___. → bedroom

title: Colours and Size

revision.summary: Describe things using colours and size words.
examples: She is wearing a small hat.
This is a very big house.
The shirt is too short for him.
He has a tall, dark green bike.

body_content:
Colours and Size

Common colours: red, blue, green, yellow, black, white. Common size words: big, small, long, short, tall. Adjectives usually go before the noun (a big red bag).

Examples

  • I have a blue bag.
  • She is wearing a small hat.
  • This is a very big house.
  • The shirt is too short for him.
  • He has a tall, dark green bike.

Quick check

  1. The sky is ___ (colour). → blue
  2. Opposite of small: ___ → big
  3. Put in order: bag / red / big → a ___ ___ bag → big red

title: Body and Appearance

revision.summary: Name parts of the body and describe what people look like.
examples: She is short with curly hair.

body_content:
Body and Appearance

Common body parts: head, hand, arm, leg, eyes, hair. To describe appearance, use "He/She has..." for features (has brown hair) and "He/She is..." for height/build (is tall).

Examples

  • She has long black hair.
  • He has blue eyes.
  • I hurt my leg.
  • He is tall and thin.
  • She is short with curly hair.

Quick check

  1. She has brown ___. (hair colour) → hair
  2. Describe height: He ___ tall. (has/is) → is
  3. Describe a feature: She ___ blue eyes. (has/is) → has

title: Food, Meals and Cooking

revision.summary: Name common foods and meals, and talk about simple cooking.
examples: We usually have rice for dinner.
He boils the eggs for ten minutes.

body_content:
Food, Meals and Cooking

Meals: breakfast, lunch, dinner. Common foods: bread, rice, chicken, vegetables, fruit. Simple cooking verbs: cook, boil, fry, cut. Use "for breakfast/lunch/dinner" to say what you eat at a meal.

Examples

  • I have toast for breakfast.
  • We usually have rice for dinner.
  • She is cooking chicken.
  • First, cut the vegetables.
  • He boils the eggs for ten minutes.

Quick check

  1. What do you eat in the morning? → ___ → breakfast
  2. Boil, fry or cut: ___ the onions → cut
  3. I have eggs ___ breakfast. (for/at) → for

title: Transport

revision.summary: Name types of transport and say how you travel somewhere.
examples: I go to work by bus.
He rides his bike to school.
They flew by plane to Spain.

body_content:
Transport

Common transport: car, bus, train, bike, plane, on foot. Use "by" with most transport (by bus, by car) but "on foot" for walking.

Examples

  • I go to work by bus.
  • She travels by train.
  • We go there on foot.
  • He rides his bike to school.
  • They flew by plane to Spain.

Quick check

  1. How do you travel? ___ car (by/on) → by
  2. Walking = ___ foot (by/on) → on
  3. I go to school ___ bike. (by/on) → by

title: Health, Feelings and Emotions

revision.summary: Talk about how you feel and simple health problems.
examples: They are excited about the trip.

body_content:
Health, Feelings and Emotions

Use "I feel..." or "I'm..." + adjective for feelings (happy, sad, tired, sick) and "I have a..." for a symptom (a headache, a cold).

Examples

  • I feel tired today.
  • She is very happy.
  • He has a headache.
  • I'm not feeling well.
  • They are excited about the trip.

Quick check

  1. I ___ tired. (feel/have) → feel
  2. She has a ___. (headache/happy) → headache
  3. Opposite of happy: ___ → sad

title: Clothes and Street Directions

revision.summary: Name common clothes for different weather, and follow simple street directions.
examples: Wear a coat — it's cold today.
Go straight on, then turn right.

body_content:
Clothes and Street Directions

Common clothes: shirt, trousers, jacket, shoes, hat. Choose clothes for the weather (a coat for cold weather). Direction words: turn left/right, go straight on, at the corner, next to.

Examples

  • Wear a coat — it's cold today.
  • Turn left at the corner.
  • Go straight on, then turn right.
  • The bank is next to the pharmacy.
  • She is wearing a red jacket and black shoes.

Quick check

  1. Cold weather → wear a ___ → coat
  2. Give a direction: ___ left at the corner. (turn/go) → turn
  3. Continue forward: go ___ on. (left/straight) → straight

title: Greetings and Introductions

revision.summary: Greet people and introduce yourself and others using Hello/Hi, I'm..., This is..., and How are you?
examples: Hi, I'm Anna. What's your name?
How are you? — Fine, thanks. And you?

Examples

  • Hello! Nice to meet you.

  • This is my friend, Tom.
  • How are you? — Fine, thanks. And you?

title: Personal Information

revision.summary: Ask and answer questions about personal information, and fill in a simple form with name, nationality and address.
examples: What's your name? — My name is Carla.
Where are you from? — I'm from Brazil. I'm Brazilian.
What's your address? — 12 Green Street, London.

body_content:
Personal Information

Use question words with be/do to ask about name, age, country and address. Nationality words (Brazilian, Japanese) describe where someone is from. This lesson also practices filling in a simple form — name, nationality, address — the same information used in real forms like a hotel registration.

Examples

  • What's your name? — My name is Carla.
  • Where are you from? — I'm from Brazil. I'm Brazilian.
  • How old are you? — I'm 25.
  • What's your address? — 12 Green Street, London.
  • Form: Name: ___ / Nationality: ___ / Address: ___

Quick check

  1. Ask about someone's country. → Where are you from?
  2. Fill in a mini form with your own name, nationality, address.
  3. Answer "How old are you?" with your own age.

revision.summary: Ask about prices and buy things politely using How much is/are...? and I'd like...
examples: How much is this T-shirt? — It's $15.
How much are these shoes? — They're $40.

body_content:
Shopping and Prices

Use How much is/are...? to ask price and I'd like... to ask for something politely.

Examples

  • How much is this T-shirt? — It's $15.
  • How much are these shoes? — They're $40.
  • I'd like a coffee, please.
  • Can I pay by card?
  • That's too expensive.

Quick check

  1. Ask the price of a bag. → How much is this bag?
  2. Ask for a coffee politely. → I'd like a coffee, please.
  3. Answer for shoes that cost $40. → They're $40.

title: Describing People and Objects

revision.summary: Describe people's appearance and objects using adjectives, with adjectives before the noun.
examples: This is a big, old house.

body_content:
Describing People and Objects

Use be + adjective to describe, and have/has for hair/eyes. Adjectives usually go before the noun (small red bag, not red small bag).

Examples

  • She is tall and friendly.
  • He has short black hair.
  • It's a small red car.
  • They are young and kind.
  • This is a big, old house.

Quick check

  1. Describe someone's hair. → She has long brown hair.
  2. Describe an object's colour and size. → It's a small blue bag.
  3. Put in order: red / small / bag → small red bag

title: Telling the Time and Routines

revision.summary: Tell the time (o'clock, half past, quarter to/past) and describe daily routines with Present Simple.
examples: What time is it? — It's half past seven.
We go to bed at 11 at night.

body_content:
Telling the Time and Routines

Use It's + time (o'clock, half past, quarter to/past). Use Present Simple with time expressions for routines.

Examples

  • What time is it? — It's half past seven.
  • I get up at 7 o'clock.
  • She has breakfast at 8.
  • We go to bed at 11 at night.
  • It's quarter to nine.

Quick check

  1. Say the time 3:30. → It's half past three.
  2. Complete: "I ___ up at seven." → get
  3. Say the time 8:45. → It's quarter to nine.

title: Frequency and Duration

revision.summary: Say how often you do something (adverbs of frequency) and for how long (for/since).
examples: I go swimming twice a week.
She studies English for one hour every day.

body_content:
Frequency and Duration

Use adverbs of frequency (always, usually, sometimes, never) for how often. Use for + a length of time and since + a starting point for duration.

Examples

  • I go swimming twice a week.
  • She studies English for one hour every day.
  • We have lived here since 2019.
  • He never eats breakfast.
  • They usually work from 9 to 5.

Quick check

  1. Say how often you brush your teeth.
  2. Complete: "I have lived here ___ 2019." → since
  3. Complete: "She studies ___ two hours." → for

title: Likes, Dislikes and Opinions

revision.summary: Talk about likes and dislikes with like/love/hate + -ing, and give opinions with I think...
examples: I like pizza, but I don't like fish.
I think this film is great.

body_content:
Likes, Dislikes and Opinions

Use like/love/hate + -ing or + noun. Use I think... to give an opinion.

Examples

  • I love swimming.
  • She hates cooking.
  • I like pizza, but I don't like fish.
  • I think this film is great.
  • What do you think of this song?

Quick check

  1. Say something you love doing.
  2. Give an opinion about a film. → I think it's good.
  3. Complete: "She ___ (not like) coffee." → doesn't like

revision.summary: Talk about past experiences using the Past Simple, regular and irregular verbs.

body_content:
Talking About the Past

Use Past Simple (regular -ed, irregular verbs) with time expressions like yesterday, last week, in 2020.

Examples

  • I visited Paris last year.
  • She went to the cinema yesterday.
  • We didn't watch the match.
  • Did you see that film?
  • He was born in 1998.

Quick check

  1. Complete: "I ___ (visit) Rome last summer." → visited
  2. Complete: "She ___ (go) to school yesterday." → went
  3. Ask about a past holiday. → Where did you go on holiday?

title: Invitations: Inviting, Accepting, Refusing, Thanking

revision.summary: Invite someone (Would you like to...?), accept (Yes, I'd love to), refuse politely, and say thank you.
examples: Would you like to come to my party?
I'm sorry, I can't. I'm busy that day.
Thank you so much for the lovely dinner.

body_content:
Invitations

Invite with Would you like to...? Accept with Yes, I'd love to. Refuse politely with I'm sorry, I can't because... Thank with Thank you for...

Examples

  • Would you like to come to my party?
  • Yes, I'd love to!
  • I'm sorry, I can't. I'm busy that day.
  • Thanks for inviting me.
  • Thank you so much for the lovely dinner.

Quick check

  1. Invite a friend to dinner. → Would you like to come to dinner?
  2. Accept an invitation. → Yes, I'd love to.
  3. Politely refuse. → I'm sorry, I can't.

title: Requests, Offers and Permission

revision.summary: Make polite requests (Could you...?), offers (I'll...), and ask permission (Can I...?).

body_content:
Requests, Offers and Permission

Use Can/Could you...? for requests. Use I'll... or Would you like...? for offers. Use Can/May I...? for permission.

Examples

  • Could you help me, please?
  • Can you pass the salt?
  • I'll carry your bag.
  • Would you like some tea?
  • Can I open the window?

Quick check

  1. Ask someone to close the door politely. → Could you close the door, please?
  2. Offer to help someone. → I'll help you.
  3. Ask permission to leave early. → Can I leave early, please?

title: Instructions and Suggestions

revision.summary: Give instructions with imperatives, and make suggestions with Let's.../Why don't we...?/How about...?
examples: Press the green button to start.
Why don't we watch a film?

body_content:
Instructions and Suggestions

Use imperatives for instructions (Turn left, Press the button). Use Let's..., Why don't we...? or How about...? for suggestions.

Examples

  • Turn left at the corner.
  • Press the green button to start.
  • Let's go to the beach.
  • Why don't we watch a film?
  • How about pizza for dinner?

Quick check

  1. Give a direction instruction. → Turn right.
  2. Suggest an activity with "Let's." → Let's go for a walk.
  3. Suggest with "How about...?" → How about coffee?

title: Future Arrangements

revision.summary: Talk about future arrangements already planned, using Present Continuous.
examples: We're having dinner with friends on Friday.
What are you doing this weekend?
She's flying to Spain next week.

body_content:
Future Arrangements

Use Present Continuous for fixed future arrangements (I'm meeting her tomorrow).

Examples

  • I'm meeting Ana at 6 tomorrow.
  • We're having dinner with friends on Friday.
  • What are you doing this weekend?
  • She's flying to Spain next week.
  • Are you free on Saturday?

Quick check

  1. Complete: "I ___ (meet) John tomorrow." → am meeting
  2. Ask about someone's weekend plans. → What are you doing this weekend?
  3. Complete: "She ___ (fly) to Rome on Monday." → is flying

examples: I work as a waiter in a restaurant.
I have two years of experience.
I am looking for a job in a shop.
Why do you want this job? — I like working with people.

body_content:
Applying for a Job

Use I am a.../I work as a... for job titles. Use Present Simple for duties, Past Simple for job history. Useful phrases: I have experience in..., I am looking for...

Examples

  • I am a teacher.
  • I work as a waiter in a restaurant.
  • I have two years of experience.
  • I am looking for a job in a shop.
  • Why do you want this job? — I like working with people.

Quick check

  1. Say your job (or a job you'd like).
  2. Complete: "I ___ (have) two years of experience." → have
  3. Answer: "Why do you want this job?"

title: Writing a Postcard

revision.summary: Write a short, simple postcard about a holiday: a greeting, short news, and a closing.
examples: I'm having a great time in Spain!
The weather is sunny and hot.
We are visiting the beach every day.

body_content:
Writing a Postcard

A postcard has three parts: a greeting (Dear.../Hi...), short news about the place, weather or activities, and a closing (See you soon! / Love,...). Keep sentences short and simple.

Examples

  • Dear Sara, / Hi Sara,
  • I'm having a great time in Spain!
  • The weather is sunny and hot.
  • We are visiting the beach every day.
  • See you soon! / Love, Anna.

Quick check

  1. Write a postcard opening line. → Dear ___,
  2. Write one sentence about the weather.
  3. Write a closing line. → See you soon!

Present Simple
